paper_b.title: A short proof of Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Both papers establish Brooks' theorem, but with fundamentally different techniques. Paper A gives an algebraic proof via the Alon-Tarsi polynomial method, using Eulerian-subgraph parity counts together with a structural lemma producing an even induced cycle with at most one chord; this yields the stronger list-degree-colorability and degree-paintability statements. Paper B gives a short combinatorial induction on $|V(G)|$ using a maximal-path / PathColor argument and a case split on whether the path covers all vertices; it then extends to correspondence (and signed-graph) coloring. The shared anchor is Brooks' theorem itself; everything else is independent machinery.

matches.explanation: Both nodes are the classical Brooks' theorem (Brooks 1941): a connected graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ is $\Delta$-colorable unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle. Paper A states it as a cited external result; paper B states it as the main theorem to be proved. Same statement up to the standard formulations (`$\Delta$-colorable' vs `$k$-colorable with $\Delta(G)\leq k$ and no $K_{k+1}$').

Paper A's corollary CP409.1 is the list-and-paintable strengthening of Brooks' theorem; it implies (and is the contribution-side counterpart of) Brooks' theorem itself. Paper B's TP419.1 is just the classical (non-list) Brooks. They play the same role on each side as `the Brooks-type statement we deliver', but paper A's version is strictly stronger (list / paintable), so the match is analogous rather than exact.

Both are the paper's headline generalization of Brooks. Paper A's TP409.4 strengthens Brooks to list-degree-colorability and degree-paintability (lists of size $\deg(v)$, with the more permissive non-Gallai-tree hypothesis). Paper B's TP419.2 strengthens Brooks to correspondence coloring (DP-coloring) with $|L(v)|=k$ under the standard $\Delta\leq k$, no-$K_{k+1}$ hypothesis. Both are `the strongest statement this paper proves about Brooks-style coloring', but the generalization axes are different (degree-list / paintability vs correspondence / signed); analogous in role, not in formulation.

These are the central proofs of Brooks-style theorems in the two papers. Paper A's PP409.3 reduces to constructing an orientation with each out-degree $\geq 1$ and differing even/odd Eulerian-subgraph counts, then invokes Alon-Tarsi (TP409.1) and the paintability analogue (TP409.2). Paper B's PP419.1 inducts on $|V(G)|$, reduces to $k$-regular, picks non-adjacent neighbours $x,y$ of a vertex $v$, builds a maximal path $P$, and case-splits on whether $P$ covers all vertices. Same target theorem, completely disjoint proof strategies; this is the AP signal at the proof-graph level.

Composite L2-vs-L2 entry under the parent proof match (PP409.3 <-> PP419.1). The two step DAGs do not have step-by-step counterparts: paper A's steps are (1) reduce to orientation existence, (2) apply structural lemma, (3) build vertex ordering via contracting $C$, (4) define orientation with $C$ cyclic and remaining edges backward, (5) enumerate Eulerian subgraphs, (6) invoke Alon-Tarsi / paintability. Paper B's steps are (1) base case + reduce to $k$-regular, (2) pick non-adjacent neighbours and build maximal path, (3) case split, (4) Case 1: $r=n$ via PathColor, (5) Case 2: $r<n$ extracting back-edge cycle $C$, (6) Case 2: bridge to $G'$ and finish coloring. Both decompose `prove Brooks' into setup + structural choice + coloring/finishing, which is the only honest analogy; emitted as a single composite per the L2 rule.

Paper A's DFS/spanning-tree ordering lemma (LP409.2) and paper B's algorithm step ASP419.1 (build a DFS tree and label vertices) both rely on the same folklore observation: a connected graph admits a vertex ordering rooted at a chosen vertex in which every non-root vertex follows a neighbor. Paper A uses it as a stand-alone lemma inside the algebraic proof; paper B uses it as the first step of the linear-time algorithm derived from its proof. Cross-type (lemma <-> algorithm_step) but the underlying structural fact is identical; flagged low-confidence because the parent constructs (algebraic proof vs DFS algorithm) differ greatly.

Paper A's `list degree colorable' (DP409.5) and paper B's generic `list coloring' (DP419.2) are both list-coloring notions, but with different list-size regimes: paper A allows $|L(v)| = \deg(v)$ (degree-sized lists), while paper B's definition fixes $|L(v)| = k$. Same conceptual root (Erdos-Rubin-Taylor list coloring), different specialisations; analogous rather than exact.

Paper A's structural lemma `every connected non-Gallai-tree graph contains an induced even cycle with at most one chord' is the technical heart of the algebraic proof and has no analogue in paper B, which does not use Gallai trees, induced cycles, or chord counts. Paper B reaches a Brooks-type conclusion via maximal-path / induction instead.
`Even Eulerian subgraph' is a paper-A-specific notion needed for the Alon-Tarsi machinery; paper B uses no oriented-graph or polynomial-method concepts.
`Odd Eulerian subgraph' is paper-A-specific (Alon-Tarsi parity counting); no counterpart in paper B.
$(k+1)$-paintability via the Paint-Correct game is a paper-A-specific notion; paper B does not consider on-line / paintability strengthenings.
Gallai trees parametrise the hypothesis of paper A's main result; paper B's hypothesis is the standard `no $K_{k+1}$, $\Delta\leq k$', so Gallai trees do not appear.
`Degree paintable' is the paintability analogue of `list degree colorable' specific to paper A; paper B has no paintability content.

The PathColor procedure (sequential greedy coloring along an uncolored path leaving the last vertex uncolored) is the central combinatorial primitive of paper B's short proof and accompanying algorithm. Paper A's algebraic / Alon-Tarsi argument uses no greedy-along-path mechanism.

Paper B's $O(m+n)$ DFS-based Brooks-coloring algorithm is a paper-B-specific algorithmic contribution derived from its inductive proof. Paper A delivers no algorithm and is concerned with existence (via polynomial-method tools), not with constructive coloring procedures.

Proof of paper A's structural lemma LP409.1 (chord and parity analysis on the shortest non-complete non-odd-cycle inducing cycle). LP409.1 itself has no analogue in paper B, so neither does its proof.

Short proof of paper A's DFS ordering lemma LP409.2 via a rooted spanning tree. The folklore fact also underlies paper B's DFS-tree algorithm step ASP419.1, but paper B never states or proves it as a stand-alone lemma; we therefore do not pair the proofs.
Internal claim inside paper A's structural-lemma proof: existence of a cycle inducing neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle. Specific to the chord/parity argument; no analogue in paper B.
Internal claim inside paper A's structural-lemma proof: the shortest such cycle of length $\geq 5$ has no universal vertex. Specific to paper A's machinery; no counterpart in paper B.
Internal claim: each vertex of the shortest such cycle is incident with at most one chord. Part of paper A's chord-bookkeeping; no analogue in paper B.
Internal claim: the shortest non-complete non-odd-cycle inducing cycle is even. Used to feed Alon-Tarsi parity counts; no counterpart in paper B.
Internal claim: the shortest such cycle has at most one chord in total. Combines with Claim 4 to deliver paper A's structural lemma; no counterpart in paper B.
